article.articleHeadline: 6.7 Million Indonesians Have Hepatitis B: Here Are the Symptoms and How to Prevent It.
article.articleSummary: Indonesia faces substantial hepatitis burden with about 6.7 million people infected with hepatitis B and 2.5 million with hepatitis C. Among hepatitis types, B and C are most common in the country and can progress to chronic infection or liver cancer. Hepatitis A and E spread via contaminated food or water, while B and C transmit through blood and other body fluids; hepatitis D can infect only those with hepatitis B and can worsen disease. Prevention differs: hepatitis B vaccination is available and emphasized for newborns and high-risk adults; Hepatitis C has no vaccine, so prevention centers on avoiding exposure to infected blood and shared syringes, razors, and unsterile equipment. Treatments vary: A and E typically self-resolve; hepatitis C is curable in over 95% of cases with early treatment; hepatitis B and D require long-term, guideline-based care. Early detection and vaccination are urged to reduce hepatitis burden.

He praised the provincial health office for extending TB tracing into sub-districts and said the CKG program broadens access to rapid, affordable health evaluation and treatment. The visit also reviewed Remedi portable digital radiography equipment from South Korea, intended to speed diagnosis in hospitals and field settings. Central Jakarta Deputy Mayor Eric P.Z. Lumbun noted strengthening TB tracing as part of Jakarta’s goal to become TB-free and welcomed distribution of Remedi units to sub-district health centers once deliveries begin. Officials urged residents suspected of TB to complete treatment and maintain healthy practices.

article.articleHeadline: Tuberculosis and Tips for Completing Treatment!
article.articleSummary: Indonesia ranks second globally in tuberculosis cases, behind India, and aims to eliminate TB by 2030. The Health Ministry prioritizes TB control and strict treatment monitoring to prevent defaults and transmission, extending care from hospitals to primary health facilities. Pulmonary TB treatment lasts six months uninterrupted; extrapulmonary TB (bone TB, tuberculoma cerebri, TB meningitis, etc.) may require up to 18 months, with evaluation for extension. Diagnosis combines clinical assessment with a rapid molecular test to detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis in sputum, supported by radiology. TB is airborne, with transmission most likely in enclosed, poorly ventilated spaces, especially in the first two weeks of untreated cough. After diagnosis, patients should discuss duration and adherence with their physician and sign informed consent for medication adherence. An illustrative case describes a 50-year-old man with smoking and diabetes presenting weight loss and productive cough, MTB detected.

article.articleHeadline: Pharmacy Academy Urges Nigeria to Prepare Now for Next Ebola Outbreak
article.articleSummary: Nigeria must prepare now for Ebola and other emerging infectious diseases, per the Nigeria Academy of Pharmacy. In an Emergency Epidemic Preparedness Webinar, experts urged pre-emptive activation of response systems rather than waiting for suspected cases. The Ebola Task Group called for continuous testing and improvement of outbreak responses, with frontline workers already trained to respond to suspected cases. A consultant physician warned that Nigeria’s weak laboratory capacity and healthcare worker migration threaten preparedness, highlighting that Ebola cannot be diagnosed by symptoms alone and lab confirmation is essential. A pharmacy-based surveillance system was proposed, leveraging accessible community pharmacies for reporting and public education; multidisciplinary training should include cleaners and support staff. Government should begin preparedness training immediately, referencing Ebola in Congo with no vaccine. Lessons from 2014 emphasize stronger surveillance, laboratory capacity, infection prevention and control, public communication, and coordinated response.

article.articleHeadline: Lunda-Sul records first case of monkeypox.
article.articleSummary: First confirmed monkeypox (Mpox) case in Lunda-Sul province, Angola. A 42-year-old national truck driver presented with widespread vesicular lesions and was seen at Lunda-Sul General Hospital. Diagnostic samples were sent to Luanda, and mpox was laboratory-confirmed. Health authorities activated epidemiological surveillance to monitor the patient’s clinical evolution and identify direct contacts. The patient transports goods between Lunda-Sul, Moxico-Leste, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with exposure possibly linked to road-side animal meat consumption, though the infection source remains under investigation. The patient is clinically stable and receiving medical care. Officials intensified contact tracing and reinforced surveillance, training health workers to boost response capacity. Public guidance urges avoiding direct contact with suspected lesions and seeking care for compatible symptoms; cross-border vigilance near DR Congo is strengthened.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in Aru: More than sixty people sensitized to preventive measures - ACP
article.articleSummary: On 22 August 2026, in Aru's Ingbokolo area of the Adi health zone, Ituri province, northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, more than 60 people were trained on Ebola virus disease prevention. The outreach by the Association de filles-mères (AFM) and partners aims to strengthen community understanding (Zone B) and encourage early adoption of measures to limit spread. Participants were instructed in regular handwashing, use of alcohol-based hand rub, environmental hygiene, physical distancing, and avoiding smoked meat during this period. Although the Adi health zone is not currently affected by Ebola, attendees committed to applying the lessons and sustaining community sensitization. The initiative is part of International Alert's Nashiriki Masikilizano 2 project, funded by the European Union, supporting innovative women-led actions and combating rumors that Ebola exists and kills.

article.articleHeadline: DRC: In Goma, the Ebola outbreak puts cultural life on hold.
article.articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo has led to a ban on public gatherings in Goma, suspending concerts, festivals and other cultural events. Goma is a major cultural hub, hosting events such as Festival Amani, Musika Na Kipaji, the Goma Dance Festival and Kivu Fashion Week. After disruptions from the 2025 seizure of the city by M23 rebels, Ebola now imposes a new halt. The crisis has wide social and economic repercussions: livelihoods of dancers, musicians, hosts, technicians, producers, and related sectors like hotels and shops suffer, and investors have fewer incentives to fund new projects. Market vendors report slowed activity. While no new cases are reported in Goma, the outbreak continues to spread in the eastern provinces, stressing health teams in a war-weary region with millions displaced; Ebola adds another social, cultural, and economic blow to Goma.

article.articleHeadline: Tshopo: Civil society denounces the absence of preventive measures against Ebola in some schools - ACP
article.articleSummary: On August 22, 2026, in Kisangani, Tshopo Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, CONEPT-Tshopo denounced the absence of Ebola virus disease prevention measures in several schools as the province faces an Ebola outbreak. Jeanpy Atilenge urged school heads to implement barrier measures, strengthen handwashing facilities, and raise awareness among students and staff to curb transmission. With the 2026-2027 school year starting on September 1, the call emphasized a risk-free reopening. While some schools have opened for registrations, many are graduallyInstalling or reinforcing hygiene provisions, including handwashing points, awaiting further guidance from education and health authorities. CONEPT-Tshopo stressed that full adherence to preventive measures is essential to protect pupils, teachers, and the broader educational community and to enable safe schooling. CONEPT RDC, founded in 2009, advocates education for all.

article.articleHeadline: How does a clinical trial work amid the fastest Ebola outbreak in history?
article.articleSummary: MBP134 and remdesivir are being evaluated in the PARTNERS trial in the Democratic Republic of the Congo for Bundibugyo ebolavirus–positive patients, amid the eastern outbreak centered in Bunia, Ituri. Sponsored by the World Health Organization and coordinated by the National Institute of Biomedical Research (DRC), with the Institute of Tropical Medicine (Belgium) and University of Oxford, the study includes MSF and Africa CDC among partners. Participants are randomized to four arms: MBP134 plus remdesivir; MBP134 alone; remdesivir alone; or standard of care. The trial is conducted at MSF’s Elikya Ebola Treatment Center in Bunia, where eligible patients are invited to enroll. MSF provides operational support; however, WHO-led partners design and run the protocol and determine allocation. Primary aim: determine safety and efficacy to inform regulatory approvals and wider use in future Ebola outbreaks, potentially transforming outbreak response.

article.articleHeadline: Cholera in Kwango: over 1,500 cases and 102 deaths in three areas - ACP
article.articleSummary: Cholera outbreak in Kwango Province, Southwest Democratic Republic of Congo, with 1,532 cases and 102 deaths reported as of August 19, 2026 across three health zones: Popokabaka (744 cases, 25 deaths), Kasongo-Lunda (560 cases, 37 deaths), and Boko (198 cases, 40 deaths). Popokabaka shows some decline; Boko has had no new cases for two weeks, while Kasongo-Lunda remains the active hotspot, with recent deaths linked to interruptions in care and limited prevention uptake. An importation of cases from Angola is reported in Kasongo-Lunda. Provincial health authorities supplied Kasongo-Lunda with a treatment kit (lactated Ringer’s, ORS, catheters, doxycycline, ciprofloxacin, chlorine, zinc, PPE). The public is urged to practice strict hygiene, consume hot, well-cooked foods, and use treated water. The outbreak began May 24 in Popokabaka and was officially declared June 25 after INRB confirmation, later spreading to Boko and Kasongo-Lunda.

article.articleHeadline: El Niño has already arrived, and dengue looms with the coming rains.
article.articleSummary: Dengue cases in Paraguay total 293 in 2026, with three confirmed between weeks 30–32 (two in Asunción, one in Caaguazú); chikungunya remains at 19 cases, including three imported from Bolivia. The epidemiological situation is under control with low dengue circulation and an average of about 148 suspected cases weekly, though notifications are rising in Cordillera, Paraguarí, Alto Paraná, Canindeyú, Amambay, Ñeembucú, San Pedro, Caaguazú and Caazapá. El Niño is established in Paraguay, with forecasts of heavier rainfall from October to December, which could create more mosquito breeding sites. The main defense is household vector control: eliminate or cover any water-holding containers, treat pools with chlorine, and routinely empty, clean, and refill animal drinkers since Aedes eggs can cling to container walls. There have been no dengue hospitalizations or deaths in the past three weeks, and the Limpio outbreak shows no new cases.

article.articleHeadline: New Zealand Hit by Biggest Flu Outbreak in a Decade as Health System Buckles
article.articleSummary: Influenza A drives New Zealand’s flu surge in years, with Auckland flu hospitalisations at a 10-year high and infection rates at a four-year high, while RSV and COVID-19 circulate. Healthline calls rose about 20% in the past week, from roughly 1,000 to 1,200–1,300; one in five assessed are directed to hospital or emergency services. About 30% of calls concern children under five, prompting Plunket to deploy nurses. Health NZ reports system under intense pressure, with a 27% rise in staff sickness absence. A coordination centre redirects personnel; Winter Plan expands telehealth and urgent-care capabilities, while some elective procedures are canceled. About 1,500 ED visits were redirected to urgent care; 264 extra staff deployed, with 64 in additional duties. Auckland remains hardest hit, with long waits and ward upgrades delayed; wards for Middlemore, Wellington, and Waikato not expected until next year, with Hawke’s Bay capacity next month and Nelson in November.

article.articleHeadline: Baguio records 125 mild COVID‑19 cases, no deaths
article.articleSummary: 125 COVID-19 cases in Baguio City as of Aug 17, with 120 recoveries and five active cases, all mild. Most infections were mild and the majority of residents affected were vaccinated; 99% of recovered patients were vaccinated. A substantial share of cases occurred among health workers under regular testing for infection prevention. No Cicada COVID-19 subvariant has been detected in Baguio. Across the Cordillera Administrative Region, DOH tallies 184 cases from January–August 2026, with Baguio accounting for 129, followed by Benguet (39), Mountain Province (7), Kalinga (4), Apayao (2), Ifugao (2), and Abra (1). Officials urged continued vigilance around seniors, children, pregnant women, and people with comorbidities, citing vaccination as protection against severe disease.

article.articleHeadline: Kaohsiung City Reports Two New Imported Dengue Fever Cases Among Migrant and Fishing Workers; Preventing On-Campus Transmission From Imported Cases; Deputy Mayor Inspects Campuses and International Student Dormitories for Epidemic Prevention
article.articleSummary: Two new imported dengue fever cases were reported in Kaohsiung City, Taiwan, bringing the 2026 total to 18 imported cases. One case involves a Filipino migrant worker who arrived on Aug 16 and worked at a Luzhu District factory from Aug 18; he developed headache and fever on Aug 20, with NS1 rapid test and PCR both positive. The other case is a Filipino fishing worker who tested negative on a hospital rapid test during a medical check but yielded a positive PCR result on Aug 21. In response, authorities expanded case investigations, executed vector surveillance, eliminated breeding sources, and conducted chemical control around residence/work sites. Deputy Mayor Li Huan-ren visited Cheng Shiu University of Technology and Chung-Shan Industrial & Commercial College on Aug 19 and 21 to enforce: inbound NS1 rapid testing within 3 days, 14 days of health monitoring, and campus environmental cleanup with enhanced mosquito barriers. A dengue prevention rewards program extends through year-end: 500 NT$ vouchers for residents, university staff/students, new residents and families; 200 NT$ vouchers for re-entry migrant workers. Emphasis on protecting campuses and communities amid seasonal rainfall.»

article.articleHeadline: Dissemination of sanitary measures for the prevention of trichinellosis in different regions of the country.
article.articleSummary: Senasa (Argentina’s National Service for Agri-Food Health and Quality) conducted a territorial outreach campaign on trichinellosis across major Argentine provinces as of 2026-08-22, delivering talks, presentations, and educational materials to producers, food processors, students, and the general public. Activities occurred in towns including General Madariaga and Tornquist (Buenos Aires); Puerto Esperanza (Misiones); Nogoyá and Santa Elena (Entre Ríos); Realicó and Santa Rosa (La Pampa); Río Colorado and General Conesa (Río Negro); Sarmiento (Chubut); Río Gallegos (Santa Cruz); Rosario (Santa Fe); plus Córdoba and Mendoza. The campaign emphasized prevention of Trichinella infection via consumption of undercooked or raw pork products. Training with bromatology offices in Salto (Buenos Aires) and Puerto Madryn (Chubut) supported inspectors and students. Mendoza and Córdoba hosted technical meetings; emphasis for small/medium pork producers on sanitation, animal nutrition, and meat analysis by Artificial Digestion. Recent cases have been reported; winter increases transmission risk. Contact +54 9 11 35859810 or the Trichinellosis quick guide.

article.articleHeadline: Imus City urges residents to join daily cleanup efforts to combat dengue
article.articleSummary: Imus City reports a dengue surge with 192 confirmed cases, 46 probable, and 53 suspected as of Aug. 20, 2026, up from 186 confirmed cases on July 29. By Aug. 19, the total confirmed cases stood at 192. Barangays with the highest counts are Buhay na Tubig (25), Bucandala 1 (20), Pasong Buaya II (18), Carsadang Bago 2 (12), and Malagasang 1-G (11). Authorities promote daily cleanup under the Alas-Kwatro Kontra Mosquito program at 4 p.m. to search and destroy breeding sites such as containers, drains, pots, and tires, and caution against relying on fogging alone since eggs and larvae may persist. Public guidance includes using mosquito repellent, wearing long, light-colored clothing, and maintaining a clean environment. Health officer Dr. Ferdinand Mina lists symptoms as high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle/joint pain, vomiting, fatigue, and rash; seek hospital care for severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, or breathing difficulties. Drinking adequate water is advised.

article.articleHeadline: Shared risk: Cattle, humans can give each other 'TB' | John Eiron R. Francisco
article.articleSummary: The Philippines should launch a national bovine TB eradication program led by the Bureau of Animal Industry, in coordination with DOH, DOST, and other agencies, to curb zoonotic transmission. A Bukidnon study of 275 slaughtered cattle found 126 positives for bovine TB and post-mortem lesions across ages and sexes, suggesting under-detection. PSA data show 2.52 million cattle as of 2026-03-31, down 1.5% from 2025, with smallholders making up 86.4% and Northern Mindanao and Calabarzon as leading regions. Bovine TB spreads to humans via inhalation or consumption of contaminated products; human TB is primarily caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. In the United States, Mycobacterium bovis accounts for under 2% of human TB cases, reflecting cattle-control programs and pasteurization. Proposed measures include better slaughterhouse surveillance with rapid diagnostics, standardized post-mortem exams, mandatory reporting, PPE for workers, and stronger vet–physician–community coordination.

Bolivia reports no Ebola cases to date and maintains preventive measures to prevent entry and spread. The drill aims to measure reaction times and determine areas needing strengthening.

article.articleSummary: Rabies vaccination campaign targets dogs and cats in Corumbá and Ladário, Mato Grosso do Sul, on the Brazil–Bolivia border, starting 22 August 2026, with parallel actions in Assis Brasil, Epitaciolândia, Brasiléia (Acre), Cáceres (Mato Grosso), and Guajará-Mirim (Rondônia). Conducted by the Ministry of Health, the campaign distributes vaccines and information materials and strengthens integrated rabies surveillance in border areas with high cross-border animal movement. Brazil has had no human rabies cases from dog-transmitted variants AgV1/AgV2 in a decade. The most recent human case in Mato Grosso do Sul was in 2015 in Corumbá (38-year-old man bitten by a dog; died after hospital care). Rabies persists in wildlife—bats, primates, foxes. article.articleHeadline: Businesswoman Who Died After Plastic Surgery Had an Infection Before the Procedure
article.articleSummary: Andreia Vieira Gaspar, a 51-year-old Brazilian businesswoman living in Spain, died after six facial cosmetic procedures in Goiânia, Goiás, Brazil. Family reports preoperative infection signals; Spain-based tests reportedly identified bacteria and active infection, shared with the surgical team, but the operation proceeded. She traveled from Spain for six facial interventions, including hairline alterations, repositioning of facial tissues/muscles/chin, removal of excess skin and periocular fat, neck/jaw fat removal, and autologous stem cell treatment. Surgeries lasted more than eight hours. Postoperatively, she developed severe tongue swelling and had difficulty closing her mouth; about six hours later her condition worsened. A medical report cited acute thrombosis and pulmonary infarction as death causes. She died on August 12. The Goiás Public Prosecutor's Office opened an inquiry, with possible involuntary homicide; Cremego and the hospital are reviewing preoperative, surgical, and postoperative care.

article.articleHeadline: Drought may bring monkeys, mosquitoes, and yellow fever closer to Brazil's cities
article.articleSummary: Yellow fever resurfaced in Brazilian cities beginning in late 2016, with Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro, and São Paulo reporting over 2,000 cases and more than 700 deaths. A drought-driven mechanism suggests thirsty howler monkeys and marmosets moved toward urban areas, followed by Haemagogus forest mosquitoes capable of long-distance flight, increasing human exposure. The drought was 9.5% more extreme than a once-in-a-century event, with dry air potentially increasing mosquito biting frequency. A mathematical model including two mosquito species, howler monkeys, marmosets, and people was calibrated to Minas Gerais data. Only the full version—featuring both animal movement and variable biting—reproduced the epidemic, scoring about 0.90 accuracy. Haemagogus dominated transmission; Aedes aegypti infections were rarely detected. Vaccination remained the strongest mitigating factor, though even near-universal vaccination did not fully prevent a second wave; insecticide or conservation alone were insufficient.

article.articleHeadline: UFPI and CIATEN Strengthen the Fight Against Chagas Disease in the Cocais Region.

Seven municipalities sent managers, health professionals, researchers and representatives to participate in a Deliberative Dialogue, part of the PPSUS-supported project Síntese de Evidências Sobre Doenças Determinadas Socialmente. The initiative linked synthesized evidence with local context to shape practical health actions for prevention, diagnosis, care and control, with equity at the center due to social and territorial disparities in access. Participants reviewed the evidence, debated feasibility and acceptability, and identified barriers and opportunities for implementation. The outcome was locally adapted directions to inform decision-making, strengthen Chagas disease responses, and translate research into policy and action in the Region of Cocais, through science-to-territory integration.

article.articleHeadline: Alert: the lettuce parasite that causes explosive diarrhea affects thousands of people.
article.articleSummary: Cyclospora cayetanensis is driving a cyclosporiasis outbreak in the United States with more than 27,000 infections linked to contaminated lettuce. Infected individuals report explosive watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, nausea, extreme fatigue, and weight loss; symptoms can persist for weeks with relapses if untreated. Transmission stems from ingestion of water or raw produce washed inadequately, and person-to-person spread is uncommon due to the parasite’s environmental maturation. The outbreak is centered in Michigan and neighboring Midwest states; the United Kingdom has 67 cases in travelers who had visited Mexico and returned in 2026. A suspected lettuce source from Taylor Farms distributed to Taco Bell ties the U.S. outbreak to a retail supply. Brazil faces low import risk as it does not source fresh greens from the U.S./Mexico; diagnosis requires special stool stains or PCR tests, and underdetection is likely.

article.articleHeadline: 44 cases of Guinea worm disease in Vietnam: Warning about the risk from natural water sources.
article.articleSummary: 44 cases of Guinea worm disease (dracunculiasis) have been documented in Vietnam since 2020, with Lao Cai Province reporting 27 cases, Phu Tho 14, and Thanh Hoa 3. On August 19, 2026, a patient at Dang Van Nguu Hospital was diagnosed, raising the national total to 44. Transmission is linked to natural water sources in midland/forested areas where people drink from streams; the parasite is acquired via water containing infected Cyclops water fleas. Consumption of undercooked wild animals such as frogs, snakes, and other wildlife may contribute. Surveillance is ongoing but remains challenging and largely passive; authorities call for stronger surveillance, community education, and improved water, sanitation, and animal management. Measures include secure household water, wastewater management, deworming of dogs/cats, and behavior changes to avoid drinking natural water in forest settings. Key questions remain about Vietnam-specific species and reservoirs.

article.articleHeadline: Urgently prevent hand, foot, and mouth disease ahead of the new school year.
article.articleSummary: HFMD outbreak in Dong Nai City, Vietnam, totals nearly 9,000 cases with 1 death since 2026, 1.75 times higher than the same period last year. Over 96% are school-age children in preschools. Cases remain elevated during summer break, approaching alert level. The EV71 virus is circulating amid hot, humid weather; delayed parental reporting may raise risk as students return. Ahead of the 2026-2027 school year, authorities urge joint action: schools and local health services should coordinate with district health stations, sanitize classrooms, toilets, toys, and surfaces; share class lists for surveillance; and educate staff and parents. Daily health monitoring is required; suspected cases should trigger immediate isolation and notification of parents and the health station. Enforce the "3 clean" rule—clean eating, clean spaces, and clean hands—and ensure water and soap. Early detection and rapid response are essential to prevent transmission.

article.articleHeadline: Parasites causing anemia and malnutrition in children.
article.articleSummary: In Vietnam's tropical climate, parasites cause anemia and malnutrition in children. The article lists soil-transmitted helminths—Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm), Trichuris trichiura (whipworm), hookworms, Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm), and Strongyloides stercoralis (threadworm)—along with food-borne liver, lung, and intestinal flukes and various tapeworms. Zoonotic larvae from dogs and cats include Toxocara spp., Gnathostoma spp., Taenia solium larvae, and rat lungworm Angiostrongylus cantonensis, plus other twisting nematodes. Protozoa such as Entamoeba histolytica and Giardia duodenalis cause diarrhea and malabsorption. Disease ranges from abdominal pain and diarrhea to chronic malnutrition, iron-deficiency anemia, stunting, and impaired growth and development; some larvae migrate to liver, lungs, or central nervous system, with ocular involvement possible. Transmission occurs via ingestion of eggs/larvae from soil, water, or undercooked produce, hand-to-mouth contact, and skin penetration. Prevention emphasizes regular deworming, handwashing with soap, wearing shoes, cooking meat thoroughly, washing produce, and proper pet waste management.

article.articleHeadline: Starting today, the free oral cholera vaccination program has begun.
article.articleSummary: From 22 August 2026, Bangladesh launches the Preventive Oral Cholera Vaccination Campaign-2026, offering free vaccination nationwide to curb cholera. The first-dose phase runs through 21 September, with the second-dose phase from 26 September to 25 October (14 days apart). The program aims to immunize 5.175 million people aged 1 year and older, excluding pregnant women, across 14 high-risk upazilas and police thana areas. In Dhaka, Dhaka South City Corporation will vaccinate about 1.17 million people at 192 centers across 17 wards (Lalbagh, Gundaria, Kadamtoli, Kamrangirchar). Dhaka North City's Shere Bangla Nagar, Khilkhhet and Tejgaon, plus parts of Munshiganj, Kishoreganj, Narayanganj and Brahmanbaria districts, will also participate. The campaign was inaugurated by Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md. Sakawat Hossain at the DSCC Auditorium, with DSCC Administrator Md. Abdul Salam; Tejgaon program was also attended by State Minister Dr. M. A. Muhit. Full protection requires two doses and should be paired with safe water and hygiene measures.

article.articleHeadline: Raw sprouts under scrutiny in the United States: 55 cases of Escherichia coli and Salmonella, the alert extends to 15 states.
article.articleSummary: US FDA reports an outbreak linked to alfalfa sprouts with 55 people sick across 15 states as of 21 August 2026, including four hospitalizations and no deaths. Cases comprise 46 infections with Shiga toxin–producing Escherichia coli, seven with Salmonella Agona, and two with both pathogens. Separately in Europe, EFSA and ECDC describe a multi-country Salmonella Bovismorbificans ST377 outbreak linked to alfalfa sprouts; 109 cases in ten EU/EEA countries plus the United Kingdom between January and May 2026, with 18 hospitalizations and Finland recording a death and a probable second. Investigations trace contamination to alfalfa seed lots sourced from India, passing through Italian suppliers before distribution. Sprouts’ warm, moist germination conditions promote pathogen growth; washing is insufficient. Cooking sprouts until steaming hot reduces risk; risks are higher for children, the elderly, pregnant women, and immunocompromised individuals. No confirmed link between US and EU outbreaks.

article.articleHeadline: Special camp to detect elephantiasis among North Indian workers near Tiruchendur.
article.articleSummary: Near Tiruchendur, Tamil Nadu, a midnight blood-collection camp was held in Veerapandiya Pettai to preemptively screen North Indian migrant workers employed at a private star-hotel construction site for elephantiasis (lymphatic filariasis). District Health Officer Dr. Yazhini authorized the drive, with local health oversight. Public health inspector Aristattil and health inspectors Rajesh, Muthuramaran, and Mugil from Kayalpattinam collected blood samples at midnight, when nocturnal microfilariae are most detectable. All samples have been sent to laboratories for analysis; results, once available, will guide medical advice and provision of anti-filarial treatment or preventive measures for those testing positive. The effort aims at early detection and management, ensuring appropriate care for infected individuals and steps to prevent further transmission. Processing continues with laboratory confirmations pending.

article.articleHeadline: MCD Takes a Major Step to Prevent Dengue and Malaria: Mosquito Terminator Train Runs on the Railway Track
article.articleSummary: Delhi's MCD and Northern Railways launched the Mosquito Terminator Train 2026 at New Delhi Railway Station to curb malaria and dengue by spraying anti-larval agents along track-side water-collecting spots. The 75-km operation will cover rail corridors and surrounding areas, deploying power spray tanks to the sides of tracks. Planned routes include New Delhi–Sahibabad; Adarsh Nagar–Badli; Delhi Junction–Delhi Shahdara; Hazrat Nizamuddin–Lajpat Nagar; Sarai Rohilla–Patel Nagar–Safdarjung; Kishan Ganj–Sadar Bazaar–Delhi Cantt; and Palam–Gurgaon–Faridabad–Okhla–Tuglakabad. The campaign runs through September 2026. Dengue infects about 390 million people annually worldwide, underscoring the public health rationale of reducing breeding sites and protecting Delhi from vector-borne diseases such as malaria and dengue.

article.articleHeadline: Outbreak of disease in the Baiga belt of Balaghat, controversy over death toll figures.
article.articleSummary: Balaghat district's Baiga belt in Madhya Pradesh faces an outbreak of malaria and measles across numerous villages in the Birsa block. Official government data record eight child deaths, while opposition Congress alleges 19, highlighting alleged undercounting as families describe unregistered losses. Reported cases include Mangli, a seven-year-old from Gathiya village who died after ambulance arrival on August 11; Baran Singh's six-year-old Ronu, who died at home after fever and dysentery before reaching hospital; and five-year-old Rianish from Ghummar who died August 20. Authorities have not accepted these deaths in the tally. Laboratory-confirmed measles infections have been found in affected children who missed routine immunization; malaria is also reported. A measles-rubella vaccination drive begins August 20 for children 9 months to 10 years. Health surveillance continues; 207 hospitalizations, 163 recoveries, 44 in hospital, 3,329 tests with 704 positives. Contention over nutrition support and ration distribution persists, with local MLA demanding accountability.

Dr. Ankit Agarwal links the surge to temperature swings that accelerate viral infections, especially among children, the elderly, and those with weak immunity; fever and water-borne diseases are noted risks in this season. Doctors are counseling preventive measures, including drinking boiled water and maintaining hygiene. Distant patients arriving in crowds have strained health services. Dr. Ashish Srivastav notes rising monsoon-related viral infections and diarrhea, advising boiled water, freshly cooked meals, and avoidance of openly sold street foods.

article.articleHeadline: 12-year-old boy dies of cerebral malaria at JSR hospital, kin allege negligence | Ranchi News

article.articleHeadline: Malaria, Kala Azar show sharp decline in India: Report
article.articleSummary: India's NVBDCP Annual Report 2025-26 shows strong progress against Malaria, Kala Azar, and Lymphatic Filariasis under national elimination programmes. Kala Azar elimination threshold (<1 case per 10,000 population) was achieved in 2023 across 633 blocks in 54 districts spanning four states and has been sustained. Malaria cases declined 78.15% and malaria deaths 77.60% from 2015 to 2024, with 160 districts in 23 states reporting zero indigenous malaria for three consecutive years since 2022, qualifying for Sub-National Verification for Malaria Elimination. India exited the High Burden to High Impact (HBHI) list in 2024 per World Malaria Report 2025 and remains on track to achieve a 75% reduction by 2025 (70%+ in 2024). Lymphatic Filariasis elimination targets microfilaria rate <1%. In 2025, MDA achieved 94% coverage across 111 districts/696 blocks in 13 states (February); the August round reached 95% in 50 districts/394 blocks in four states, signaling strengthened transmission interruption.

article.articleHeadline: Fungal infections are now causing more deaths than malaria and tuberculosis combined, and the blame lies with humanity.
article.articleSummary: Fungal infections now cause about 3.8 million deaths annually worldwide, up from ~2 million in the 2010s, surpassing malaria and tuberculosis in mortality. Underdiagnosed mycoses, notably those due to Aspergillus fumigatus and Aspergillus flavus, disproportionately affect patients with asthma, tuberculosis, or lung cancer, and complicate pneumonia and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease outcomes. David W. Denning of the University of Manchester, publishing in The Lancet Infectious Diseases, synthesizes data from more than 85 articles across around 100 countries, highlighting the global burden and interactions with HIV/AIDS, where roughly half of AIDS deaths may be fungal-related. A COVID-19-era surge of mucormycosis in India underscores emergent risk. Early diagnosis and effective treatment are critical, yet many countries lack adequate diagnostic capacity, and antifungal resistance is rising. While mortality rises may reflect population growth and better estimation, improvements in detection could reduce deaths in the future.

article.articleHeadline: Shigellosis cases open up a new AMR challenge in Keralam
article.articleSummary: Shigellosis in Keralam faces rising antimicrobial resistance, with primary antibiotics for community-acquired cases losing efficacy. KARS-Net data (since 2023) show ciprofloxacin resistance at 96% and ceftriaxone resistance at 36%. Community-acquired AMR now concerns treatment outside hospitals. Clinicians warn that shrinking antibiotic options jeopardizes management of severe dysentery, where patients may progress to septic shock or multiorgan failure; ceftriaxone may be unreliable, forcing consideration of meropenem in critical cases. Shigella transmission remains food- and water-borne, making it a sentinel AMR indicator for community trends. A major outbreak in June this year tallied 225 cases and six deaths across Kozhikode, Malappuram and Wayanad. Keralam has historical ESBL-producing strains and prior MDR patterns; a 2018 Government Medical College Alappuzha study reported 91.6% MDR among isolates and Ceftriaxone/Cefotaxime resistance. Most diarrhoea is self-limiting, but vulnerable groups require antibiotics.

article.articleHeadline: Any contact is a Level-III exposure! Carrying a large viral load, now at its peak, appearing in many regions — NetEase Mobile.
article.articleSummary: Rabies alert in Beijing as bat intrusions into homes rise this summer. From May 1 to Aug 18, 2026, Fengtai District Fire Rescue logged 203 bat-disturbance calls, nearly double the 102 recorded in the same period last year. Urban ecological improvements and warm, rainy conditions are boosting bat activity; East Asian bats roost in building gaps and vent ducts, entering apartments via unsealed air-conditioning openings or torn screens. Direct contact with a bat is categorized as Level-III exposure (highest risk) for rabies, even without obvious wounds. A recent case involved a person struck in the face by a bat, treated with five rabies vaccines and six-dose passive immunization around the exposure site. Immediate guidance: rinse exposed areas with soap and running water for about 15 minutes, disinfect with iodine, and seek urgent evaluation at a rabies post-exposure clinic for PEP. Do not handle bats; ventilate rooms and seal gaps.

article.articleHeadline: Dangerous viruses in the laboratory, the risk of reopening the biosafety case.
article.articleSummary: Bat-borne coronavirus HKU5-CoV-2, a merbecovirus related to MERS, can use the human ACE2 receptor and infect various human cells in culture, signaling a potential spillover risk even if not currently capable of causing a new pandemic. A Lancet Microbe review (2000-2021) identified 309 laboratory-acquired infections and 16 accidental pathogen releases, suggesting that even elite facilities are prone to errors and that reporting may be incomplete. The debate focuses on experiments that enhance dangerous traits—transmission or virulence—and weighs surveillance and preparedness against the risk of catastrophic accidents. In the United States, a July 20, 2026 policy sets bans, risk assessment requirements, oversight, and possible suspensions for federally funded high-risk research. Regarding COVID-19's origin, WHO's 2025 SAGO report favors zoonotic spillover but cannot exclude a laboratory incident due to data gaps from China. The lesson: monitor viruses in nature and tighten laboratory biosafety.

article.articleHeadline: One shot covers three serotypes! Ruip Biotech's cattle and sheep trivalent foot-and-mouth disease vaccine officially launched
article.articleSummary: As of 2026-08-22, Ruip Biotech Co., Ltd. officially launched Ruifejing Tri-valent Foot-and-Mouth Disease Inactivated Vaccine, co-developed with the National Animal Disease Prevention and Control Center core team. The vaccine protects cattle and sheep against three circulating serotypes—O Ind2001, A SEA97, and SAT1—addressing the inadequacy of traditional bivalent vaccines. Marketed as 'one shot covers three serotypes,' it uses a five-level ultra-purification system with CIP/SIP online sterility control, suitable for pregnant dams and weaned calves. Following multi-regional field trials and robust safety/stability data, it obtained an official production license. Experts note that multivalent vaccination and high-purity purification can reduce stress-related losses and costs. The product targets northern pasture areas, large dairy farms, meat sheep operations, and cross-province flocks, with broad domestic demand; ongoing surveillance will guide iterations, per President Xu Lei.

article.articleHeadline: ScienceNet - Unveiling the Secret of How Foot-and-Mouth Disease Virus Hijacks Host Energy
article.articleSummary: Foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV) hijacks host energy metabolism in livestock by activating two autophagy pathways that together boost glycolysis and viral replication. Researchers from the Lanzhou Veterinary Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, China, showed that FMDV simultaneously triggers a selective autophagy route dependent on specific host target proteins and mitophagy, creating a robust metabolic drive for infection. When one pathway is blocked, the other maintains high glycolytic flux, illustrating a dual-pathway safeguard that enhances viral survival in pig, cattle, and sheep cells. Reported in Autophagy and published on 23 August 2026, the work identifies molecular targets within host–autophagy–metabolism crosstalk, offering avenues for host-targeted antiviral strategies and the development of small-molecule therapeutics and new animal disease control agents. This finding underscores a novel mechanism by which FMDV leverages host energy systems to sustain propagation, relevant to global livestock health.

article.articleHeadline: Cholera Returns to Yangon: Over 500 Hospitalizations and a Lesson That Also Concerns Europe.
article.articleSummary: Cholera returns to Yangon, Myanmar: since August 9, at least 500 people hospitalized for severe diarrhea; tests detected 149 cholera positives, while the National Health Laboratory confirmed nine Vibrio cholerae infections. The outbreak surged with over 100 admissions on August 13, then declined. A 92-year-old died after hospitalization for diarrhea; authorities cited preexisting cardiac and respiratory conditions as the cause. Cholera spreads via contaminated water and food and can cause profuse watery diarrhea, dehydration, and shock within hours, though early rehydration can save severe cases. The crisis reflects infrastructure collapse after five years of civil war, compromising water, sanitation, waste collection, and access. WHO: by May 31 Myanmar had 205 watery diarrhea cases, 272 by June 28; globally in June, over 47,000 cholera/acute watery diarrhea cases and 354 deaths. The episode shows cholera as a disease of fragile systems; Europe should note prevention starts with water, sanitation, hygiene, and detection.

article.articleHeadline: 11 million measles cases expected worldwide in 2026... What has brought the disease back into the spotlight?
article.articleSummary: 11 million measles cases are projected worldwide in 2026, with outbreaks across Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas. Most infections will occur in low- and middle-income countries, though high-income nations are also affected. WHO cites Africa and Asia as the center of transmission, yet outbreaks have hit Europe and the Americas as well. Notable affected areas include Burundi, Democratic Republic of Congo, Somalia, Sudan, and Yemen; outbreaks also in Maldives and Zambia, with rising cases in India. Bangladesh reports the year’s deaths exceed 900, worsened by political turmoil since 2024 reducing vaccination uptake. In the Americas, Canada lost measles-free status in November 2025; Mexico and the United States risk doing so too, while Guatemala records over 30,000 cases in 2026. Vaccination remains essential: Europe’s one-dose coverage about 94% and two-dose about 88%; LMICs ~80% and ~70%. COVID-19 disrupted supply/services, underscoring the need for funding and rebuilding trust to reach >95% coverage and protect zero-dose children.
